slides.heading: Oral Lesson
bullets: The words boy, girl, city, book, and desk are all names of objects.
Each of these words is a name — and a word that is a name is called a Noun.
We can name a person (John), a place (Chicago), or a thing (railroad).
Whenever we name something we can see or think about, we are using a noun.

slides.heading: The Word and the Idea
bullets: “Language is the expression of thought by means of words.” A word, then, is a sign — it is not the thought itself.
Three things stand apart: the word (the sign), the idea it calls to mind (the concept), and the thing the idea is true of.
“dog” — the word is three letters; the concept is “a four-footed domestic animal”; the thing is the animal in the yard.
The tie between a word and its concept is fixed by agreement, not by nature — so it can change.
We reason with the concepts, not the letters; so we must know which concept a word carries.

slides.heading: Word Shift Example
bullets: Marriage:  “the legal union of a man and a woman for life, as husband and wife”  →  “a legal union between two people.”
Woman:  “an adult human female”  →  “an adult who lives and identifies as female, regardless of sex assigned at birth.”
Vaccine:  “a substance containing a killed or weakened pathogen that produces immunity to a specific disease”  →  “…that produces an immune response or protection to a specific disease.”

slides.heading: Common & Proper Nouns
bullets: A Common Noun fits any one of a whole class:  boy, city, river, dog.
A Proper Noun names one particular person, place, or thing:  John, Chicago, the Mississippi.
Test — “boy” fits every boy, so it is common; “John” names one boy, so it is proper.
Rule — a proper noun always begins with a capital letter (and so do I and O).
A common noun starts with a small letter, unless it begins a sentence.

slides.heading: Practice — Common or Proper?
slides.instruction: Tell whether each noun is common or proper.

slides.heading: Number — One, or More Than One
bullets: Number is the property of a noun or pronoun that shows whether it stands for one, or for more than one.
Singular Number denotes but one object:  fan, book, boy.
Plural Number denotes more than one:  fans, books, boys.
It is a property of the word, not a count of the world:  class (singular) names many;  scissors (plural) names one.
A verb has no number of its own — it only agrees with its subject:  “The bird sings,” but “The birds sing.”

slides.heading: Making Plurals — the Main Rules
bullets: Most nouns — add s:  book → books,  girl → girls.
After s, ss, sh, ch, x, or z — add es:  church → churches,  box → boxes,  mass → masses.
y after a consonant — change y to i, add es:  city → cities,  lady → ladies.
y after a vowel — just add s:  monkey → monkeys,  day → days.
o after a consonant — add es:  potato → potatoes,  hero → heroes.  (But o after a vowel, and musical terms, add s:  cameo → cameos,  piano → pianos.)

slides.heading: Making Plurals — f, Irregulars & Special Cases
bullets: f or fe → ves:  knife → knives,  calf → calves,  leaf → leaves.  (But some just add s:  roof → roofs,  chief → chiefs,  safe → safes.)
Irregular, by a change of form:  man → men,  woman → women,  foot → feet,  tooth → teeth,  goose → geese,  mouse → mice,  child → children,  ox → oxen.
The same in both numbers:  sheep,  deer,  trout,  swine,  vermin.
Letters, figures, and signs — add ’s:  two b’s,  three 7’s,  +’s.
Compound nouns — make the chief word plural:  spoonful → spoonfuls,  son-in-law → sons-in-law,  passer-by → passers-by.

slides.heading: Abbreviations
bullets: An Abbreviation is a shortened way of writing a word.
A period marks the shortening:  Doctor → Dr.,  Mister → Mr.,  Number → No.
Most abbreviations begin with a capital letter.
Many come from Latin:  A.M. (ante meridiem),  P.M. (post meridiem),  A.D.,  N.B.,  ult.,  prox.
Some use two or more capitals with periods:  U.S.,  P.O.,  C.O.D.

slides.heading: Abbreviations — Titles, Rank & Office
bullets: Titles:  Dr. (Doctor),  Mr. (Mister),  Mrs. (Mistress),  Esq. (Esquire),  Rev. (Reverend),  Hon. (Honorable),  Prof. (Professor).
Rank & office:  Gen. (General),  Gov. (Governor),  Col. (Colonel),  Maj. (Major),  Capt. (Captain),  Supt. (Superintendent),  Atty. (Attorney),  Admr. (Administrator).
By initials:  M.C. (Member of Congress),  M.D. (Doctor of Medicine).

slides.heading: Abbreviations — Places, Time & Commerce
bullets: Places:  St. (Saint / Street),  Mt. (Mount),  Co. (Company),  P.O. (Post Office),  R.R. (Railroad),  U.S. (United States).
Time & Latin:  A.M. (forenoon),  M. (noon),  P.M. (afternoon),  A.D. (in the year of our Lord),  B.C. (before Christ),  N.B. (take notice),  ult. (last month),  prox. (next month).
Commerce & notes:  No. (Number),  Lb. (Pound),  Bbl. (Barrel),  C.O.D. (Collect on Delivery),  P.S. (Postscript).

slides.heading: Contractions
bullets: A Contraction joins two words and drops some letters.
The apostrophe ( ’ ) marks the spot where letters are left out.
do not → don’t   ·   we are → we’re   ·   I have → I’ve
it is → it’s   ·   they are → they’re   ·   over → o’er
An abbreviation is shortened with a period; a contraction, with an apostrophe.

slides.heading: The Parts of a Sentence
bullets: Every declarative sentence asserts something about something; it encodes a proposition.
The Subject is that of which something is affirmed — what the proposition is about:  “Ice is cold.” → Ice.
The Predicate is that which is affirmed of the subject:  “Ice is cold.” → cold.
The Copula is the word that joins the predicate to the subject and makes the assertion:  is.
Copula means “link.” It is usually a form of the verb be — is, was, will be.
Note: when we analyze sentences, we will treat “sentence” as short for “declarative sentence.”

slides.heading: Subject & Predicate — the Thing, Not the Word
bullets: A sentence is the words; the proposition is the thought they express (Lesson 1).
The subject is that of which something is affirmed — the thing or notion spoken of, not the word that names it.
In “Ice is cold,” the subject is ice (the notion meant); the word “Ice” is only its sign.
It is the notion, not the object: “Unicorns are mythical” has a subject, though no unicorn exists.
So “Ice is the subject” is shorthand — we name the subject by the word that carries it.

slides.heading: The Predicate & Quality-Words
bullets: The predicate often names a quality of the subject:  “Man is mortal.” → mortal.
Quality-words tell what kind the subject is:  soft, wise, sweet, round, happy.
A noun can be the predicate too — then it tells the class:  “Horses are animals.” → animals.
So a predicate may be a quality (adjective) or a class (noun).

slides.heading: Analysis
bullets: An Element is one distinct part of a sentence.
The Subject and Predicate are the Principal Elements — no sentence can be formed without them.
All other parts are Subordinate Elements. The copula is not itself an element — it only asserts.
Analysis is the separation of a sentence into its elements.
Model — “Iron is heavy.” →  Iron | is : heavy   (subject | copula : predicate).
The divider after the subject crosses below the line; a lighter divider sets the copula off from the predicate.

slides.heading: Analyze — Diagram the Sentence
slides.instruction: Separate each sentence into subject | copula : predicate. The divider after the subject crosses below the baseline; the copula is set off from the predicate, since it is not itself an element.

slides.heading: Analyze — More Sentences
slides.instruction: Separate each sentence into subject | copula : predicate. Note that the predicate may be a quality (adjective) or a class (noun) — the copula only asserts it of the subject.
